content.body:
I owe an apology to every woman I've treated for low ferritin in the last 14 years.

I didn't know it at the time. I do now. And I can't keep quiet about it anymore.

I'm a primary care doctor. 14 years in practice.

In that time, I've prescribed ferrous sulfate to thousands of women. Maybe more.

The protocol was always the same. Ferrous sulfate. 325mg. Take it with vitamin C. Come back in three months.

That was my training. That was the standard of care. I never questioned it.

Until last year, when it happened to me.

Heavy periods for years had finally caught up. I was losing hair faster than I could pretend it wasn't happening. My ponytail was half the size it used to be. I could see my scalp through my part in certain lighting and I'd rearrange my hair to hide it.

The exhaustion was worse. By 2pm every day I was done. Not tired — done. Like my body was filled with cement.

I'd sit in my car after work for twenty minutes before leaving because I didn't have the energy to drive.

So I got my blood work done. Ferritin: 9.

I wasn't surprised.

So I did what I'd told hundreds of patients to do. Ferrous sulfate. 325mg. Twice a day with vitamin C.

My own prescription. The one I'd handed out a thousand times.

By week two my stomach was destroyed. Constipation so bad I was hiding in the toilet between appointments. Nausea every morning. Bloating that made me unbutton my pants at my desk.

I told myself what I'd told every patient who complained: push through. The side effects are normal and nothing to worry about.

Five months later I got retested.

Ferritin: 15.

Six points. In five months.

I stared at those results at the same desk where I'd told women "give it more time" and "ferrous sulfate is the gold standard."

For the first time, I understood exactly how they felt when I said that.

I'd done everything right. Followed my own protocol perfectly. And my ferritin barely moved while my hair kept falling out and my body was still running on empty.

That's when I started thinking something was wrong with me. That I just couldn't absorb iron. That this was just my body now.

A doctor. Blaming her own body.

In 14 years of practice, I know exactly what it means when a treatment fails across multiple patients. It means the treatment is wrong. Not the patient.

And here I was, failing on the same treatment I'd given hundreds of women — and my first instinct was to blame myself.

How many of my patients did the same thing?

That question kept me up all night.

I sat at my kitchen table at midnight and started reading. Not the prescribing guidelines I'd memorized in residency. The actual research.

What I found made me sick.

Ferrous sulfate absorbs at approximately 15%. That means 85% of every pill just sits in the gut. That's the constipation. That's the nausea. That's the bloating I'd been telling women to "push through."

But that wasn't even the worst part.

Iron bisglycinate — a chelated form that absorbs through a completely different pathway — has been available for years.

And the research shows it absorbs up to four times better than ferrous sulfate. And it doesn't destroy your stomach because it bypasses the gut lining entirely.

This form existed the entire time I was prescribing ferrous sulfate.

But absorption of iron is only step one. The body has to STORE it as ferritin. And to do that, it needs specific cofactors — vitamin C, B6, B12, and folate to convert iron into stored ferritin.

Without them, iron has nowhere to go. Your ferritin doesn't move.

For 14 years, I prescribed the cheapest, worst-absorbing form of iron on the market. And when my patients told me it wasn't working, I told them to take more.

I called a colleague in hematology the next morning. Told her what I'd found.

She wasn't surprised.

"We've known about this for years. Bisglycinate with cofactors is what the research supports. I don't know why primary care still starts with ferrous sulfate - it's no good."

That sentence broke something in me.

A blood specialist knew. Had known for years. And it never reached the doctors actually writing the prescriptions.

Because the protocols haven't been updated in decades. Because we spent less than two hours on iron supplementation in medical school.

So women keep suffering through months of stomach pain on iron and we kept telling them to push through because that's what we were taught.

I spent the next two weeks looking at every iron supplement I could find. Most had the same problem — better forms of iron, but still just iron by itself. No cofactors. Still only doing step one of three.

I was about to give up and piece it together from four or five separate bottles when I finally found one that had everything in a single formula.

The right form of iron. Vitamin C. B6. B12. Methylfolate in the active form. Copper.

And two ingredients I'd never seen in any iron supplement before.

Lactoferrin — a protein that directs iron into ferritin storage.

And L-lysine — an amino acid shown to raise ferritin in women who didn't respond to iron alone. That research was published in 2002. Over twenty years ago.

I ordered it that night once I cross-checked the formula with the research.

Week 2. No stomach issues. After five months of misery on ferrous sulfate, I almost didn't trust it.

Week 4. The 2pm crash disappeared. I stopped sitting in my car after work.

Week 6. I washed my hair and barely anything came out. The shedding had slowed dramatically.

Week 8. Baby hairs along my temples.

Week 12. I got tested.

Ferritin: 72.

15 to 72 in twelve weeks.

I felt like a completely different person. The exhaustion that had made my body feel like cement for over a year — gone. I had energy past lunch for the first time in years. I could think clearly again.

And my hair. I could run my fingers through it without a handful coming out. The gaps along my part were filling in. My ponytail had weight to it again. I looked in the mirror and recognized myself again.

But then the guilt hit.

I sat in my office and thought about every woman who'd sat across from me at that desk.

The woman who came back three times saying the iron wasn't working. I told her to give it more time.

The women who said it was destroying their stomach. I told them the side effects were normal.

The women who stopped coming back entirely. They probably gave up.

I'm not prescribing ferrous sulfate anymore. Every woman in my practice with low ferritin is now taking this same formula - bisglycinate with cofactors. Ferritin levels I couldn't move in six months are resolving in as little as eight weeks.

I wasn't a bad doctor. I was a misinformed one. But my patients were the ones who suffered.

If your ferritin is low and you've been on ferrous sulfate for months with barely any movement — it's not you.

It's the iron.

I've linked the supplement I took — and what I now give to my patients — below:

👉 https://nivara-shop.com/products/ferravital-ferritin-support

P.S. — I think about the women who stopped coming back. The ones who decided they couldn't take iron and gave up. If you're one of them — it wasn't your fault. You were given the wrong iron.

P.P.S. — Give it 4 weeks minimum. That's when the energy comes back. By week 6-8 the shedding slows. They have a 90-day money-back guarantee if your ferritin doesn't improve.

content.body:
After 15 years as a dermatologist, I watched Sarah sit in my office crying.

She'd spent two years trying to stop her hair falling out. Tried biotin. Tried collagen. Tried every expensive shampoo she could find.

Her doctor ran blood tests. Everything came back normal.

But her hair kept falling out in clumps.

I finally asked her the one question nobody else had:

"When was the last time someone checked your ferritin?"

She looked at me like I was speaking another language.

My name is Dr. Emma Chen. I'm a board-certified dermatologist and I've treated over 8,000 women with hair loss.

And here's what most doctors miss.

Sarah was 34. Healthy. Doing everything "right."

But her hair was falling out in clumps. Every morning. Clumps in the drain. Clumps on her brush. Her ponytail used to be thick. Now she could wrap her fingers around it twice. She'd stopped wearing it down because she could see her scalp.

And she was exhausted. The kind of tired where your whole body feels like cement. Crashing by 2pm. Coffee doing nothing.

Her doctor checked her iron. Said it was normal.

But she never checked her ferritin — her iron storage. That's a completely different number.

I tested it. The result came back: 13.

Normal range technically starts at 12. But hair needs ferritin above 70 to grow properly.

Sarah's hair wasn't falling out because of stress. It wasn't genetics.

Her hair was starving. And nobody had checked.

When ferritin drops too low, your body goes into survival mode. Your heart needs iron. Your brain needs iron.

Your hair? Not essential.

So your body steals iron from your follicles to keep you alive. That's why the shedding won't stop. That's why you're exhausted. Same cause.

I started testing ferritin on every woman who came in with hair loss.

Over twelve months, I tested 214 women. 187 had ferritin below 50.

87%.

All had been told they were "fine."

But here's where it gets worse.

Most iron supplements don't fix it.

Ferrous sulfate — the cheap kind doctors prescribe — only absorbs at 15%. The rest wrecks your stomach. Constipation. Nausea. And your ferritin barely moves.

Liquid iron — gentler, but doses are tiny. Women take it for months and their levels go up 3 points.

I saw it constantly. Women trying iron, getting sick or seeing no results, giving up. Hair still falling out.

Then I discovered why.

Iron bisglycinate absorbs 4x better with no stomach issues. But it needs vitamin C, B6 and B12 alongside it — otherwise your body can't store it as ferritin.

Most supplements have one or the other. Almost none have everything.

I spent weeks looking for something I could actually recommend.

That's when I found FerraVital.

Chelated iron bisglycinate. Vitamin C. B6. B12. Even wholefood beetroot iron. Everything the research says is needed. Nothing unnecessary.

I started recommending it to patients whose ferritin was stuck. The women who'd tried everything. The women who couldn't tolerate other iron.

Sarah was one of the first.

Week 4: The afternoon crashes stopped. She had energy past 2pm for the first time in years.

Week 6: The shedding slowed. She washed her hair and didn't see clumps in the drain. She wasn't terrified to brush it anymore.

Week 8: Baby hairs. Tiny ones at first, around her hairline. Then more.

Week 12: We tested again. Ferritin was 74.

Thirteen to seventy-four in twelve weeks.

She sat in my office and cried again. But different this time.

"I feel like myself again. I actually recognise myself."

I've now recommended FerraVital to over 400 women.

Michelle, 38: "My ferritin went from 16 to 71. My hair finally stopped falling out after two years."

Jessica, 42: "I'd given up on iron because it destroyed my stomach. This one didn't. My hair is thicker than it's been in years."

Rebecca, 29: "Three doctors told me it was stress. My ferritin was 11. Nobody checked."

The pattern is always the same.

Dismissed. Told they were fine. Watched their hair fall out and blamed themselves.

If your hair is falling out and you're exhausted all the time — your ferritin is probably in the teens.

That's not normal. That's not stress. That's not ageing.

Your hair is starving.

Don't wait until you can see your scalp.

Don't wait until you've cried more this year than the last five combined.

Don't wait until you don't recognise yourself anymore.

Link's below if you want to check it out.
